title: Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard -- Ch. 11: Common Meaning of Common Words in the Constitution
keywords: Common Meaning of Common Words in the Constitution
contortive way of interpreting the Constitution
primary_topics: Chapter 11 of 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' -- CJP's long-held position that 'residence' in the Constitution's qualification for elective office should carry the common dictionary meaning ordinary people give it, namely actual, physical and personal presence, and not the technical lawyers' concept of domicile

His account of the two cases that framed the quarrel: his Dissent in Marcos v. Comelec -- the first extended Opinion he wrote as a member of the Supreme Court, promulgated fifteen days after he assumed office -- and his Separate Opinion in Domino v. Comelec, where Chief Justice Davide's ponencia reiterated that residence means domicile

A historical debunking of domicile itself: the concept arose in American conflict-of-laws cases about the estates of men who left home before steamboats and the oceanic cable, and was never intended to govern political rights, so using it for political qualifications enlarges it beyond its purpose

His constitutional-interpretation creed that the Constitution is not a lawyer's document but the people's, so its common words must be read in the sense understood by the ordinary men and women who ratified it and are required to obey it
sub_topics: He opens with the personal marker that his Dissent from the Resolution denying reconsideration in Marcos v. Comelec was the first extended Opinion he wrote as a Justice, promulgated fifteen days after he assumed office
He states the majority's rule in Marcos: when the Constitution speaks of residence in election law it actually means only domicile

He notes that Domino v. Comelec, through Chief Justice Davide Jr., reiterated the same equation of residence with domicile -- intention to reside in a fixed place plus personal presence and conduct indicative of that intention
He identifies the common issue in both cases: whether the candidate met the constitutional requirement of residence in the district for not less than one year immediately preceding the election
He restates the three-fold traditional rule of domicile the Court applied: everyone must have a domicile, it remains until a new one is acquired, and no one may have more than one at a time

He summarizes the ruling on the facts: Domino's domicile of origin was Candon, Ilocos Sur and his domicile of choice since 1991 was Quezon City, and he failed to show a new domicile of choice in Sarangani
He agrees with the result -- Domino failed the one-year residence requirement -- but disagrees with the doctrine that equates residence with domicile
He argues that the common people who ratified the Constitution would consult a dictionary rather than the journals of the Constitutional Commission, so Webster's meaning should control
He confesses that this contradicts the textbook rule taught by his political law professors, and that even as a student he frowned upon such a contortive way of reading the Constitution
He proposes the operative test: residence means actual, physical and personal presence substantial enough to show by overt acts an intention to fulfill the duties of the office sought
He answers the framers-intent objection: had they meant legal domicile they should have said so, and the people would have looked up that word instead

He traces domicile to American conflict-of-laws jurisprudence on decedents' estates in an era before steamboats and the oceanic cable, and to later conflict cases on taxation and divorce, none of them about political rights

He explains the purpose of the residence period -- to let candidates know their constituents' needs and difficulties and to let the electorate evaluate their fitness -- which the domicile rule defeats, since one may keep a legal domicile without ever setting foot in the district so long as the animus revertendi remains

He closes by quoting a decision of three decades earlier that constitutional language should be understood in its common use, and by reaffirming that Domino still failed to prove actual presence in Sarangani for a year before the 1998 elections
signature_phrases: a contortive way of interpreting the Constitution
Webster's definition of residence should be controlling
actual, physical and personal presence in the district that a candidate seeks to represent
If the framers of our basic law intended our people to understand residence as legal domicile, they should have said so.
To use it to determine qualifications for political office is to enlarge its meaning beyond what was intended
It is not a document reserved only for scholarly disquisition by the most eminent legal minds of the land.
provided one retains the animus revertendi or the intention to return

stances.claim: When the Constitution says 'residence' it should be read as ordinary lay persons read it -- actual, physical and personal presence in the district, substantial enough to show by overt acts an intention to fulfill the duties of the office -- and not as the technical concept of domicile.
stances.rhetorical_move: plain-meaning argument anchored on the dictionary and on who ratified and must obey the charter, against the textbook rule he was himself taught

stances.claim: Domicile was never designed to govern political rights; it arose in American conflict-of-laws cases about decedents' estates and was later extended to taxation and divorce, so using it for electoral qualifications enlarges it beyond its purpose and yields strained, contortive readings of the Constitution.
stances.rhetorical_move: genealogical critique: recovering the historical origin of a doctrine to show it is being used outside its field

stances.claim: The domicile test defeats the very objective of the residence requirement, because a candidate can retain legal domicile without ever setting foot in the district -- or in the country -- so long as he keeps the animus revertendi.
stances.rhetorical_move: purposive reductio: testing the rule against the purpose of acquainting officials with their constituents and the electorate with their candidates

stances.claim: Even on his own stricter reading, Juan Domino still failed, because he adduced no convincing evidence of actual, physical and personal presence in Sarangani for at least a year before the 1998 elections.
stances.rhetorical_move: concurrence in the result while rejecting the doctrine, showing the disagreement is about method rather than outcome

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 11 of 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' recorded CJP's dissent from one of Philippine election law's settled equations -- that 'residence' in the Constitution means 'domicile.' He recalled that the first extended Opinion he wrote as a member of the Supreme Court was his Dissent from the Resolution denying reconsideration in Marcos v. Comelec, promulgated fifteen days after he assumed office, and that the majority there held that when the Constitution speaks of residence in election law it actually means only domicile. In Domino v. Comelec, Chief Justice Davide Jr.'s ponencia reiterated that rule, applied the three-fold traditional test of domicile, and held that Juan Domino, whose domicile of origin was Candon, Ilocos Sur and whose 1991 domicile of choice was in Quezon City, had not established a new domicile of choice in Sarangani. CJP agreed that Domino failed the one-year requirement but rejected the reasoning. Reiterating his Marcos dissent, he argued that residence should be interpreted as ordinary lay persons understand it, since the common people who ratified the Constitution would consult a dictionary rather than the journals of the Constitutional Commission, so that Webster's definition should control and residence should mean actual, physical and personal presence substantial enough to show by overt acts an intention to fulfill the duties of the office. He admitted this contradicted the textbook rule taught by his political law professors, but said that even as a student he had frowned upon such a contortive way of interpreting the charter. He added that domicile arose in American conflict-of-laws cases about the estates of men who left home before the steamboat and the oceanic cable, and was later used in taxation and divorce cases, never to govern political rights; that the domicile test defeats the purpose of the residence period, which is to make officials acquainted with their constituents and let the electorate judge their fitness, since legal domicile survives absence so long as the animus revertendi remains; and that the Constitution, being the people's document and not a lawyer's, must be read in the sense of common use. He closed by repeating that Domino had still failed to prove actual presence in Sarangani for a year before the 1998 elections.
